content: Insulin requirements can change during pregnancy, and the most effective treatment for pre-existing diabetes in pregnant women remains uncertain. Various insulin regimens, such as those administered via syringe or pen, and different types of insulin, including fast-acting and human insulin, are available. This review aimed to evaluate the effects of different insulin types and regimens in pregnant women with pre-existing type 1 or type 2 diabetes. The search for relevant studies included databases such as the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, as well as reference lists of retrieved studies. Only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included, while quasi-randomized and cross-over trials were excluded. Data collection and analysis were conducted independently by two reviewers, and the quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. The review included five trials involving 554 women and their babies. These trials were generally of very low quality due to small sample sizes, wide confidence intervals, high or unclear risk of bias, lack of blinding, unclear randomization methods, and selective reporting of outcomes. Pooling of data was not possible because each trial examined different comparisons. 1. Lispro Insulin vs. Regular Insulin (33 women): Seven cases of pre-eclampsia occurred in the Lispro group compared to nine in the regular insulin group, with no significant difference (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.35 to 1.30). Five caesarean sections were reported in the Lispro group versus nine in the regular insulin group, with no clear difference (RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.25 to 1.39). No fetal anomalies were observed in the Lispro group, while one was reported in the regular insulin group, with no significant difference (RR 0.35, 95% CI 0.02 to 8.08). Outcomes such as macrosomia, perinatal deaths, birth trauma, and neonatal morbidity were not reported. 2. Human Insulin vs. Animal Insulin (42 women): No cases of macrosomia were reported in the human insulin group, while two occurred in the animal insulin group, with no significant difference (RR 0.22, 95% CI 0.01 to 4.30). Outcomes such as perinatal death, pre-eclampsia, caesarean section, fetal anomalies, birth trauma, and neonatal morbidity were not reported. 3. Pre-Mixed Insulin vs. Self-Mixed, Split-Dose Insulin (93 women): Two cases of macrosomia were reported in the pre-mixed insulin group compared to four in the self-mixed group, with no significant difference (RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.09 to 2.54). Seven caesarean sections for cephalo-pelvic disproportion occurred in the pre-mixed group versus 12 in the self-mixed group, with no clear difference (RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.25 to 1.32). Outcomes such as perinatal death, pre-eclampsia, fetal anomalies, birth trauma, and neonatal morbidity were not reported. 4. Insulin Pen vs. Conventional Needle (93 women): One case of macrosomia was reported in the pen group compared to five in the needle group, with no significant difference (RR 0.21, 95% CI 0.03 to 1.76). Five caesarean sections occurred in the pen group compared to 14 in the needle group, suggesting a lower likelihood of caesarean delivery with pen use (RR 0.38, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.97). Outcomes such as perinatal death, pre-eclampsia, fetal anomalies, birth trauma, and neonatal morbidity were not reported. 5. Insulin Aspart vs. Human Insulin (223 women): None of the primary outcomes, including macrosomia, perinatal death, pre-eclampsia, caesarean section, fetal anomalies, birth trauma, or neonatal morbidity, were reported. 6. Insulin Detemir vs. NPH Insulin (162 women): Three cases of major fetal anomalies were reported in the insulin Detemir group compared to one in the NPH insulin group, with no significant difference (RR 3.15, 95% CI 0.33 to 29.67). Outcomes such as macrosomia, perinatal death, pre-eclampsia, caesarean section, birth trauma, and neonatal morbidity were not reported. The authors concluded that the evidence is limited and of very low quality, with no meta-analyses possible due to the heterogeneity of the trials. As a result, no definitive conclusions can be drawn regarding the optimal insulin types and regimens for pregnant women with pre-existing diabetes. Further research is needed, including larger trials with robust randomization and blinding methods, to evaluate key outcomes such as macrosomia, pregnancy loss, pre-eclampsia, caesarean section, fetal anomalies, and birth trauma.
